title: What should you ask first in a market entry case, and which trap should you avoid?
description: The first question to ask in a market entry case, how to structure it, and the trap to avoid.
hook: Ask first what the client's goal is and over what time frame, because "should we enter?" only has an answer once you know what success means. The trap is stopping at "is the market attractive?" and forgetting how the client would enter, when, and whether to test it with a pilot first.
body:
The first question to ask

What is the goal of entering, and over what time frame?

A client chasing $50M of new revenue in five years needs a different market, and a different entry route, from one that wants a foothold to protect against a rival. The goal also sets the bar: a target margin, a payback limit or a market-share ambition. Without it you cannot say yes or no, only "it depends".

How to build your structure

  • Is the market attractive? Size and growth, margins, barriers to entry.
  • Can we win? Competitors, customer needs, our edge.
  • Will it pay? Revenue, costs, upfront investment, payback.
  • Can we pull it off? Capabilities we lack, how to enter (build, partner or buy), timing, a pilot, risks.

Every branch must feed the yes or no. The full tree is in the market entry framework.

Mini case: a coffee chain looks abroad

A UK coffee chain expects each new overseas shop to make $600k of sales a year at maturity. At a 15% operating margin, that is $90k of operating profit per shop. Opening a shop costs $450k, so simple payback is $450k ÷ $90k = 5 years.

That assumes a shop is mature from day one. Suppose it makes $45k in year one and $70k in year two before reaching $90k. Cumulative profit is $385k after five years, so payback slips to about 5.7 years. (This still ignores tax and the cost of capital; for those, see payback and NPV worked examples.)

A ten-shop rollout needs $4.5M of capital before working capital and local head-office costs. Before committing that, test the assumptions that drive the answer:

  • Are there enough sites with the footfall and rent to hit $600k?
  • Will local customers pay the assumed price for an unfamiliar brand?
  • Are there reliable suppliers and staff?

If those are uncertain, recommend a pilot: two shops, clear targets for sales per shop and margin, and a go or stop decision after enough trading data. Compare it with the alternatives too: more shops at home, or franchising abroad.

The trap most people fall into

Treating "the market is big and growing" as the answer. It says nothing about whether this client can win there profitably, how it would get in, or how to limit the downside.

Weak: "The market is growing 8% a year, so I'd recommend they enter."
Strong: "I'd enter, but through a two-shop pilot. At $90k profit per mature shop, payback is around five to six years, so the rollout only makes sense if pilot shops reach $600k of sales by year three."

Two prompts to try

Should a supermarket invest in vertical farms to grow salad near its stores?

Show the answer
  • Market: demand for fresh local salad; the price premium shoppers will pay.
  • Economics: cost per kg against buying from growers; energy prices.
  • Capability: running farms versus partnering with a specialist; technology risk.
  • Strategic value: less waste, fresher produce, supply security, carbon.

Where to start: cost per kg, especially energy, against buying from growers.

The trap: being won over by the story before checking energy costs.

Should a US pet-insurance company enter Canada?

Show the answer
  • Market: insured pets today and growth; how many pet owners are uninsured.
  • Competition: who leads, on what price and cover; how vets and pet shops sell policies.
  • Economics: premium per pet, claims ratio, cost to acquire a customer, payback.
  • Entry route: licensing and regulation in each province; build a local team, partner with a local insurer, or buy one.

Where to start: entry route. Insurance is regulated, so whether and how fast the client can get licensed shapes everything else.

The trap: assuming US pricing and claims data carry over unchanged.
